definition: A long, open, level stretch of paved or paved-and-planted ground, typically along a waterfront or in front of a large building, used for walking.
origin: From French esplanade, from Italian spianata (a level, cleared space), from spianare (to level, flatten), ultimately from Latin planus (flat). origin: A plain English compound of brown + field, coined by American environmental and planning agencies in the late 1980s and early 1990s as a direct counterpart to 'greenfield.' The colour brown honestly evokes disturbed, often contaminated industrial soil rather than the untouched green of open land.

definition: A tract of undeveloped land, typically farmland or open countryside, considered for new construction.

definition: A person travelling on foot, especially in a street or urban area shared with vehicles.
origin: From Latin pedester (going on foot, plain, prosaic), from pes, pedis (foot). English borrowed it in the 18th century first as an adjective meaning 'on foot' or, figuratively, 'dull and unimaginative,' and only later, in the 19th century, as a noun for a person walking, especially one navigating streets built for wheeled traffic.

definition: A street closed at one end, providing access from only one direction, often used to reduce through traffic in residential areas.
origin: A direct borrowing of French cul-de-sac, literally 'bottom of the sack' or 'bottom of the bag,' from cul (bottom) + de (of) + sac (sack, bag). Originally an anatomical term for a bodily pouch closed at one end, it was adopted into English street planning in the 19th century for a road with exactly the same shape, open at one end and sealed at the other.

origin: From Latin arteria, from Greek arteria (windpipe, later a blood vessel), possibly related to Greek airein (to raise) or aer (air), reflecting the ancient belief that arteries carried air. City planners borrowed the anatomical image in the 19th century, comparing a network of major roads carrying traffic to the arteries carrying blood through a body.

definition: The overall visual character and layout of a town, formed by the arrangement of its buildings, streets, and open spaces.
origin: A plain English compound of town + -scape (a view or scene, taken from landscape, ultimately from Old English sceppan, to shape). British planners and architects popularised 'townscape' in the mid-20th century, notably through the Architectural Review magazine, to describe a town's visual character the way 'landscape' describes open countryside.

definition: The extent to which an area is designed to make walking safe, convenient, and pleasant, typically judged by density, safety, and access to nearby amenities.
origin: A recent English coinage combining walk + the suffix -ability (capable of being done, from Latin -abilis).
